title: Templated perpendicular ferroelectricity in textured Aurivillius oxide-based thin films

paper_content.abstract:
The discovery of novel ferroelectric compounds and the modulation of polarization in
established ferroelectric materials have persistently represented crucial and highly dynamic
areas of research within the field of ferroelectric materials science. Here we demonstrate a
structural templating strategy to reconfigure Aurivillius-phase oxides into metastable
ferroelectric phases with tailored polarization. By stabilizing a metastable WO phase within
3
a Bi WO framework, we achieve robust out-of-plane polarization (10 µC/cm2) in textured
2 6
WO /Bi WO films, contrasting the purely in-plane polarization of pristine Bi WO . First-
3 2 6 2 6
principles calculations and atomic-resolution scanning transmission electron microscopy
unveil a WO phase with oxygen displacement-driven ferroelectricity. Prototype ferroelectric
3
field-effect transistors and memristors fabricated from these films exhibit robust switching
ratios (>106) and thermal stability up to 350°C. This work not only expands the family of
binary ferroelectric oxides but also establishes a generalizable paradigm for overcoming
polarization-directionality constraints in layered ferroelectrics.
paper_content.introduction:
Ferroelectric materials with switchable polarization are the cornerstone of emerging non-
volatile memory and neuromorphic computing technologies. While perovskite oxides (e.g.,
Pb
0.8
Zr
0.2
TiO
3
, BaTiO
3
, BiFeO
3
) are promising for their large intrinsic polarization1-3, their
incompatibility with silicon processing and depolarization field with reduced dimension hinder
integration. Two-dimensional (2D) ferroelectric materials (e.g., CuInP S 4, In Se 5,6, SnS7, SnTe8,
2 6 2 3
and sliding 2D ferroelectric materials such as WTe
2
9, hBN10, GaSe11) offer considerable
advantages for flexible device applications and the novel assembly of heterostructures, but suffer
from inadequate polarization and poor thermal stability12. Recent advances in HfO -based systems
2
have revived interest in CMOS-compatible ferroelectrics13-16, yet the wake-up effect associated
with their metastable phases persist as critical bottlenecks17-19.

Aurivillius-phase oxides present a unique opportunity to bridge these gaps. Aurivillius-phase
oxides, characterized by its layered perovskite structure with alternating bismuth oxide layers and
perovskite-like structural layers, are distinguished by their fatigue-resistant ferroelectric
switching20,21, high Curie temperature22, and remarkable oxide ion conductivity23. However, most
Aurivillius ferroelectric compounds exhibit in-plane polarization24. Bi WO (BWO), the simplest
2 6
member of this family that consists of alternating [Bi O ]2+ and [WO ]2- layers aligned along the
2 2 4
c-axis, restricts spontaneous polarization to the in-plane (ab) directions25,26. This configuration
fundamentally conflicts with the vertical polarization orientation required by mainstream device
architectures, such as ferroelectric field-effect transistors (FeFETs) and ferroelectric tunnel
junctions (FTJs).

The functional properties of ferroelectric thin films can be engineered through diverse
strategies in heterostructure design. Notable approaches include the use of vertically aligned
nanocomposites to create emergent multiferroicity27-29, the application of interphase strain to
robustly enhance ferroelectric polarization30,31, and more recently, the exploitation of the unique
electrostatic environment within Aurivillius frameworks to stabilize complex ferrielectric orders32.

In this work, we resolve this conflict through interfacial engineering: By templating metastable
WO domains within a BWO matrix, we simultaneously achieve perpendicular polarization and
3
inherited thermal robustness. First-principles calculations and atomic-resolution scanning
transmission electron microscopy (STEM) confirmed the presence of a WO
3
structure with
ferroelectric properties. This metastable WO phase, similar to HfO -based ferroelectrics, belongs
3 2
to the family of binary oxide ferroelectrics. Prototype ferroelectric field-effect transistors and
memristors fabricated from these films exhibit robust switching ratios (>106) and thermal stability
up to 350°C. Our work expands the landscape of simple-oxide ferroelectrics, showing a structural
templating strategy that can reconfigure Aurivillius oxides with controllable polarization
properties.
paper_content.results:
Pure Bi WO Thin Film
2 6
We start with pure BWO films as the control experiment. In literature reports, high quality
BWOfilms have been epitaxially grown on SrTiO (STO), LaAlO and NdGaO substrates, which
3 3 3
exhibit significant ferroelectricity with purely in-plane polarization25,26,33. BWO consists of an
orthorhombic phase structure with lattice constants a = 5.437 Å, b = 5.458 Å, and c = 16.430 Å34.
Fig. 1a shows the crystal structure of BWO as viewed from two crystallographic directions, the
black solid-line box indicates the unit cell of BWO. The STO (100) substrate possesses a cubic
lattice with the lattice constant a = 3.905 Å. To achieve lattice matching, epitaxial BWO films will
have their c-axis in the out-of-plane direction, and their ab plane rotated 45 around the c-axis,
thus aligning the [100] direction of BWO with the [110] direction of STO substrate25.

In our experiment, pure BWO films are grown on 0.7 wt % Nb-doped SrTiO (Nb:STO) (100)
3
substrates using pulsed laser deposition (PLD). The BWO thin film depicted in Fig. 1b exhibits a
thickness of approximately 40 nm. Due to the existence of epitaxial stress and the relatively small
thickness, some discontinuous voids still remain on the surface. The ferroelectric property of this
film was characterized using piezo-response force microscopy (PFSM). Figs. 1c and 1e present the
collected in-plane and out-of-plane PFM signals, respectively. Fig. 1c clearly shows a distribution
of four distinct spontaneous in-plane polarization states in the BWO thin film. In contrast, no stable
out-of-plane polarization is detected (Fig. 1e), the observed signal variations are attributed solely
to surface topography. In further experiments, voltage was applied to the atomic force microscope
(AFM) tip during scanning within the two dashed boxes (Figs. 1d and 1f). Due to the trailing
electric field from the tip slow-scan direction35-37, some of the in-plane ferroelectric polarization
states were noticeably altered (Fig. 1d). Because the electrically conductive Nb:STO substrate was
used, a vertical electric field also exists within the film. However, no change in the out-of-plane
PFM response was observed in Fig. 1f. This indicates that the pure-phase BWO thin film lacks an
out-of-plane ferroelectric polarization, corroborating with reports in previous literatures25,26,38,39.

Epitaxial textured two-component WO /Bi WO films
3 2 6
We design a nanocomposite Aurivillius oxide by adding WO component during the growth
3
of a pure BWOfilm (denoted as the WO /BWOfilm). In order to grow nanocomposite WO /BWO
3 3
films, we use two targets, a pure BWO target and a pure WO target. A 240 pulse BWO seed layer
3
was grown initially on the substrate, followed by 10 alternating cycles of WO (10 pulses/cycle)
3
and BWO (30 pulses/cycle) deposition, and subsequently terminated by 210 pulse BWO. The
resulting deposition component ration of WO : BWOis 1:7.5.
3

The atomic structure of as prepared nanocomposite WO /BWO films were studied by
3
aberration-corrected STEM, with cross-section samples cut from the as prepared film by focused
ion beam (FIB). Fig. 2a shows a typical STEM image of the cross-section of the film. The black
region corresponds to the Nb:STO substrate, with its in-plane orientation along the [100] direction.
In the film region, the darker gray contrast corresponds to the WO domains, which consist of W
3
and O atoms, while the lighter gray contrast corresponds to the BWO single-crystalline framework.
This contrast originates from the Z-contrast mechanism in HAADF-STEM imaging, where the
presence of heavy Bi (Z=83) atoms in BWO yields a stronger scattering signal than the WO phase.
3
Both the BWO and WO regions exhibit a sharp interface with the Nb:STO substrate, confirming
3
a robust epitaxial relationship. Moreover, the BWO and WO lattices are aligned well along the
3
[110] in-plane orientation (Fig. 2e).

In the BWO region, a layered lattice structure is clearly visible, with alternating bismuth-
oxygen (Bi-O) and tungsten-oxygen (W-O) layers along the c-axis. The alternation of light and
dark contrast is attributed to the differing electron scattering factors of the various atomic layers.
In contrast, the layered structure is not discernible in the WO domain. Fig. 2f provides a higher
3
magnification atomic-scale characterization of a WO region, corresponding to the energy-
3
dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) analysis of tungsten (W), bismuth (Bi) and oxygen (O)
shown in Figs. 2g-i. The EDS spectrum confirms the presence of W atoms and absence of Bi atoms
in the nanocrystal region. On the other hand, high-resolution XPS spectra (Supplementary Fig. 1)
reveals O, Bi, and W components in the nanocomposite thin film, with their binding energies
closely match those of pristine BWO phase, with no detectable W peaks corresponding to reduced
tungsten species (W4+/W5+), indicating that the nanocrystal is a pure WO phase. Raman
3
spectroscopy analysis (Supplementary Fig. 2) reveals characteristic vibrational peaks of BWO
(such as the symmetric stretching mode of WO octahedra at 797 cm-1)40 without notable shift even
6
in the presence of WO . This indicates that the primary lattice structure of BWO remains
3
unchanged by the incorporation of WO .
3

Figs. 2b-d present the fast Fourier transform (FFT) patterns derived from the Nb:STO substrate,
BWO matrix, and WO domain in Fig. 2a, respectively. Both the BWO and WO FFT patterns
3 3
exhibit a consistent 45° rotation relative to the STO substrate, confirming their shared epitaxial
relationship. The FFT pattern from the BWO region exhibit excellent agreement with the known
parameters of pristine BWO structure (Supplementary Fig. 3a). The WO FFT pattern shows
3
closely aligned symmetry and orientation with that of BWO, consistent with their structural
similarity, while differing in the absence of BWO-specific superlattice spots. This shared epitaxial
alignment, distinct from the STO substrate orientation, provides definitive evidence that the WO
3
phase grows via a structural templating effect mediated by the BWO matrix rather than through
direct nucleation on the substrate. These results indicate that our interfacial templating strategy
fundamentally alters the local chemistry, surpassing mere topotactic alignment, as manifested by
the distinct lattice modulation characteristics: the presence of superlattice spots in BWO,
originating from its commensurate Aurivillius superlattice, stands in sharp contrast to their absence
in the structurally simplified, cation-homogeneous WO
3
phase.

To further identify the atomic structure of the WO phase, we conducted structural
3
characterizations in different crystallographic directions. Figs. 3a and 3b depict the BWO and WO
3
regions from the same film in Fig. 2, but the TEM sample was cut along a different crystallographic
orientation, rotated 45 as compared with Fig. 2. Here the out-of-plane direction is aligned along
[001] and the in-plane direction along [100], respectively. In Fig. 3a, the BWO structure distinctly
shows a layered configuration, featuring alternating Bi-O layers and W-O layers along the c-axis.
The inserted theoretical crystal structure corresponds well with the atomic structure observed in
the STEM images. In contrast, the WO region lacks layering but displaying a square lattice
3
geometry (Fig. 3b). Figs. 3c and 3d show the FFT analysis corresponding to Figs. 3a and 3b, where
Fig. 3c exhibits precise congruence with the reference BWO crystallographic parameters
(Supplementary Fig. 3c). The FFT patterns of the WO phase in Fig. 3d closely resemble those of
3
BWO, apart from the absence of 32 superlattice spots caused by the periodic modulation. This
observation provides direct evidence that the WO phase grows via a structural templating effect
3
inherited from the BWO matrix. To validate the general applicability of the structural templating
mechanism, we synthesized ultrathin films by employing the identical epitaxial growth mode with
a reduced deposition dosage. The 8 nm-thick textured nanocomposite WO /BWO thin film
3
exhibits structural and compositional invariance across its engineered interfaces, as evidenced by
cross-sectional STEM analysis (Supplementary Fig. 4). Importantly, the WO phase forms a semi-
3
coherent epitaxial relationship with the BWO template, demonstrating the robustness of this
templating strategy in governing phase evolution across dimensional scales, further validating the
epitaxial growth and crystallographic alignment of the nanocomposite film.

Notably, this WO structure does not match to any existing WO phase in literature41-43,
3 3
signifying the stabilization of a metastable polymorph. While previous studies have demonstrated
that epitaxial strain from perovskite substrates can homogeneously distorts the bulk WO
3
structure44,45，the formation mechanism here is fundamentally different. This distinction can be
understood by analogy ferroelectric HfO
2
—which adopts a non-ferroelectric monoclinic P2
1
/c
phase at ambient conditions, but exhibits ferroelectricity in its metastable orthorhombic Pca2
1
phase18,46. Crucially, BWO shares this Pca2 ferroelectric space group. This structural templating
1
mechanism is further supported by X-ray diffraction (XRD) and reciprocal space mapping (RSM)
analyses. Conventional θ–2θ scans (Supplementary Fig. 5) reveal no significant peak shifts
between pure BWO and WO /BWO nanocomposite films, which is consistent with the presence
3
of nanosized WO domains whose diffraction is masked by the dominant BWO matrix. In contrast,
3
a pure WO film grown directly on Nb:STO (001) under identical conditions exhibits distinctly
3
different XRD features, corresponding to a conventional monoclinic phase47,48, which confirms
that the metastable polar phase observed in the nanocomposite is not stabilized by the substrate
alone. RSM measurements provide further insight into the strain state of the heterostructure.
Around the STO (001) reflection (Supplementary Figs. 6a,b), the WO /BWO film shows a
3
systematic shift toward lower q , indicating out-of-plane expansion. Consistently, the RSM around
z
the STO (103) reflection (Supplementary Figs. 6c,d) reveals a shift toward higher q accompanied
x
by lower q , confirming in-plane compression coupled with out-of-plane elongation. These RSM
z
results are in excellent agreement with cross-sectional STEM observations (Supplementary Fig.
7), collectively demonstrating that the BWO framework acts as an atomic-scale template, guiding
the WO into a semi-coherent, non-bulk-like configuration stabilized by the host lattice.
3

The BWO structural template provides a shared epitaxial orientation and a local chemical
environment, which directs the WO phase to nucleate and grow into nanodomains with specific
3
crystallographic characteristics, rather than forming randomly oriented or thermodynamically
stable phases. The primary role of the STO substrate is thus to enable the epitaxial growth of a
high-quality BWO template, which in turn architecturally guides the formation of this polar WO
3
phase.

The origin of ferroelectricity
The atomically-resolved TEM images suggest a straightforward structural model as shown in
Fig. 4a. In this model, each W atom is coordinated by five oxygen atoms, forming a pyramid shape,
distorted pentahedral as the structural unit. There are two different types of oxygen atoms in this
structure model. First, four O atoms are located roughly in the same plane with the W atoms (the
bottom plane of the pyramids), where each O atom connects two pyramid units, as marked by the
dotted rectangle and circle in Fig. 4a. Second, there is another O atom sitting at the top site of the
pyramid, which bonds solely to the W atom below it (marked by red arrow in Fig. 4a). In total this
configuration gives a WO stoichiometry, agreeing with our experiments. These WO pyramids
3 5
form a lattice precisely align with experimental TEM images from different views. First-principles
density functional theory (DFT) calculations verify the structural stability of this model.

Remarkably, we find that such an atomic configuration is naturally ferroelectric (FE). In Fig.
4a, all the pyramid units are pointing upward. Structural analysis reveals a Cm space group
configuration that breaks out-of-plane symmetry compared to the centrosymmetric WO
6
octahedral arrangement, generating a substantial out-of-plane spontaneous polarization of ~80
μC/cm2 (Fig. 4c). This polarization magnitude approaches that of prototypical perovskite
ferroelectrics, including BiFeO (100 μC/cm2)49,50 and significantly exceeds that of BaTiO (26
3 3
μC/cm2)51,52. More interestingly, the structural model naturally suggests the coexistence of a
paraelectric phase (PE), where half of the pyramid units are flipped (Fig. 4b). The reversed
polarization in neighboring layers results in zero net polarization in this phase. If all the pyramids
are flipped, it will result in the switching between the ferroelectric states (from FE' to FE'').

First-principles Nudged Elastic Band (NEB) simulations employing a 2×2×1 supercell unveil
a multi-stage polarization reversal pathway. Fig. 4e illustrates the energy profile for dipole
switching, where Fig. 4d shows the two states before and after flipping from FE'' to FE'. The
computed activation energy barrier for individual oxygen migration approximates 330 meV,
indicating practical feasibility for electric-field-induced polarization switching. This energy
landscape suggests that the ferroelectric transition proceeds through a concerted mechanism
involving sequential atomic displacements rather than simultaneous collective motion.
Additionally, the ferroelectricity is achieved here through oxygen sublattice engineering in a
simpler binary oxide system, different from conventional perovskites. The combination of giant
spontaneous polarization and moderate switching barriers positions this WO phase as a promising
3
candidate for non-volatile memory applications.

To further corroborate the consistency between the computational and experimental results,
we performed diffraction pattern simulations along the [1̅10] and [010] crystallographic directions
for the theoretically optimized structure. As shown in Supplementary Figs. 3b and 3d, the
simulated FFT patterns exhibit excellent agreement with the experimental data presented in Figs.
2d and 3d, validating the structural fidelity of the computational models and their alignment with
the observed lattice configurations.

Perpendicular Ferroelectricity of the textured nanocomposite WO /Bi WO film.
3 2 6
Indeed, the most remarkable finding with our textured nanocomposite WO /BWO films is their
3
robust ferroelectricity with perpendicular polarization. We employed PFM for a comprehensive
analysis of their ferroelectric response. The conductive Nb:STO substrate allows us to ground the
substrate and ensure the application of a vertical electric field to the thin films for out-of-plane
polarization measurements. A pre-designed badminton pattern was utilized during the PFM
scanning process (Fig. 5f), where white regions correspond to the application of a positive voltage
(+8 V) by the PFM tip, and black regions represent a negative voltage (-8 V). During point-by-
point scanning of the thin film surface with the AFM tip, voltages were applied according to this
pattern. Figs. 5a,b show the resulting out-of-plane PFM amplitude and phase after the electric field
was applied. Point-by-point scanning across the film surface resulted in distinct ferroelectric
domains, as observed both in the out-of-plane PFM amplitude and phase images. The amplitude
image shows minimized polarization at domain walls, which are formed between regions of
opposite polarization. Meanwhile, the phase image reveals a clear 180° phase shift between
adjacent domains, with black areas indicating upward polarization and yellow areas representing
downward polarization. Analysis of the PFM amplitude and phase data (Fig. 5c) along the red
dashed lines in Figs. 5a,b clearly indicates minimized polarization amplitude at the domain walls,
with a phase difference of 180° between the adjacent domains, thereby confirming the excellent
out-of-plane ferroelectric properties of the fabricated thin films. Supplementary Fig. 8 also
demonstrates comparable out-of-plane polarization switching characteristics in the 8 nm thick
nanocomposite film, further illustrating the low-dimensional nature of the ferroelectric thin films
constructed in this work.

In addition to out-of-plane measurements, in-plane PFM amplitude and phase images were
also recorded (Figs. 5d,e). The images demonstrate variations in in-plane ferroelectric polarization,
primarily induced by the trailing electric effect of the PFM tip during the scanning process. This
observation indicates that the thin films exhibit both out-of-plane and in-plane ferroelectric
polarization. Notably, higher-resolution imaging (Supplementary Fig. 9) confirms that the
characteristic in-plane ferroelectric domain structure of the BWO matrix remains clearly
resolvable at finer scan scales, demonstrating its preservation within the nanocomposite
architecture. Furthermore, to evaluate the stability and reliability of the ferroelectric switching, we
conducted polarization switching curve tests at a single PFM tip point (Fig. 5g). Ten consecutive
measurements revealed highly stable and repeatable ferroelectric hysteresis and butterfly loops,
with a consistent phase difference of 180° and a switching threshold voltage of approximately 4 V.
These results highlight the robust ferroelectric switching performance of the thin films.

To eliminate potential artifacts and verify the authenticity of the observed ferroelectric
properties, we performed alternating current (AC) voltage-dependent polarization switching
measurements (Fig. 5h). When the applied AC voltage exceeds 3 V, close to the threshold voltage
for ferroelectric switching, the polarization hysteresis loop collapsed, this behavior confirms the
genuine nature of the out-of-plane ferroelectric polarization in the textured nanocomposite
WO /BWO film53. Additionally, temperature-dependent polarization curve tests were conducted
3
to assess the films' thermal stability (Fig. 5i). Measurements were performed from room
temperature up to the maximum operating temperature of 250°C, where the polarization switching
curves exhibited robust stability despite minor jitter caused by temperature-induced contact
instability between the tip and the sample. These results collectively demonstrate the exceptional
durability and performance of our textured nanocomposite WO /BWO thin films under varying
3
thermal conditions.

Performance of ferroelectric FET and memristor devices made from WO /Bi WO films
3 2 6
Our textured nanocomposite WO /BWO thin films exhibit also macroscopic ferroelectricity,
3
as measured by a ferroelectric analyzer. Fig. 6a displays the measured ferroelectric hysteresis loop,
from which the key ferroelectric parameters were quantitatively extracted. Specifically, at an
applied electric field of 4 MV/cm, the film exhibits a remnant polarization (P) of approximately
r
10 μC/cm2, accompanied by a coercive field (E ) of 2.5 MV/cm. Since the out-of-plane
c
ferroelectric polarization in these films primarily originates from the WO domains, the measured
3
value is lower than that of the pure ferroelectric WO calculated in Fig. 4c (80 μC/cm2). The
3
macroscopic ferroelectric hysteresis loop serves as direct evidence for the presence of out-of-plane
polarization in the nanocomposite films, suggesting that these ferroelectric thin films hold
significant potential for applications in electronic devices.

To further showcase the potential device performance based on our films, we deposited a 5 nm
thick HfO insulating layer on the as-grown films using atomic layer deposition (to minimize
2
leakage effects during testing, the leakage currents primarily originate from oxygen vacancy
defects introduced during the growth of the oxide films, as well as conducting pathways formed
along interface within the textured film.) and subsequently transferred a monolayer MoS
2
via a dry
transfer method. Fig. 6b illustrates the schematic diagram of the complete device structure, for
which a FeFET characterization was conducted. Fig. 6c presents the double-sweep transfer
characteristics of the device, obtained by scanning the back-gate voltage (V
GS
) from −1.5 V to +5
V and then back to −1.5 V at a fixed drain voltage (V ) of 1 V. The FeFET exhibits a high on/off
DS
current ratio of 3×106, demonstrating its excellent performance. Then, we deposited gold
electrodes on the film surface to investigate the memristive effect induced by out-of-plane
ferroelectric polarization. Fig. 6d shows the schematic of the ferroelectric memristor device, while
Fig. 6e presents the current-voltage (I-V) characteristics under voltage sweeps ranging from -5 V
to +5 V. The device transits from the initial high-resistance state (HRS) to a low-resistance state
(LRS) after a 0 to +5 V sweep, maintains LRS during the subsequent +5 V to -5 V scan, and returns
to HRS from -5 V to 0 V. We further conducted high-temperature tests demonstrating robust
memristive behavior across a wide temperature range from 100°C to 350°C (Fig. 6f), highlighting
the potential of our ferroelectric thin films for high-temperature memory applications. This
comprehensive analysis highlights the promising capabilities of the fabricated textured
nanocomposite WO /BWO films for advanced electronic applications, supported by both
3
macroscopic ferroelectric measurements and device-level performance evaluations.

In summary, we demonstrate a structural engineering strategy to achieve out-of-plane
ferroelectricity in a metastable WO phase derived from the Aurivillius oxide BWO framework.
3
Through a combination experiments and first-principles calculations, we have confirmed the
existence of this previously unreported ferroelectric WO phase. The resulting textured
3
nanocomposite WO /BWO thin films exhibit both out-of-plane and in-plane ferroelectric
3
polarization, showcasing stable and repeatable switching behavior. Prototype FeFETs and
ferroelectric memristors fabricated from the films exhibit remarkable switching ratios (>106)
coupled with robust thermal stability up to 350°C. This work not only expands the family of binary
ferroelectric oxides but also provides a generalizable approach for polarization enhancement in
Aurivillius oxides and other layered ferroelectrics.
paper_content.methods:
Thin film growth
Bi WO , WO /Bi WO and WO thin films were epitaxially grown on (001)-oriented Nb:SrTiO
2 6 3 2 6 3 3
(0.7% wt. doped) substrates by pulsed laser deposition using a 248 nm KrF excimer laser. The
deposition was carried out at a substrate temperature of 750℃ under an oxygen environment of
400 mtorr. The laser energy density and repetition rate were maintained at approximately 1.4 J cm-
2 and 2 Hz, respectively. After deposition, the samples were cooled down to room temperature in
7.5 torr of O with a cooling rate of 5 °C/min.
2

Piezoresponse force microscopy (PFM)
PFM measurements were performed using an Oxford Instruments Cypher (E)S atomic force
microscope, equipped with conductive Pt/Ir-coated silicon probes. The local electromechanical
response was characterized in both out-of-plane and in-plane directions using AC excitation
amplitudes of 800 mV at frequencies of 350 kHz and 650 kHz, respectively. Litho-PFM mode was
utilized to locally pole the material and write domain patterns by applying a DC bias through the
scanning tip, enabling the assessment of polarization switching. Spectroscopic PFM (SS-PFM)
measurements were performed in dual AC resonance tracking (DART) mode. In this mode, an AC
excitation signal was superimposed on a series of DC triangular and sawtooth waveform voltages
to track the bias-dependent electromechanical response.

Scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM)
Cross-sectional specimens for STEM were prepared by focused ion beam (FIB) lift-out and
subsequently thinned using a Gatan 691 PIPS for final ion milling. High-angle annular dark-field
(HAADF) STEM imaging was performed on an aberration-corrected (scanning) transmission
electron microscope (JEOL, Grand ARM 300) operated at an accelerating voltage of 300 kV.

Materials Characterization
X-ray θ–2θ scan and reciprocal space mappings were performed using a high-resolution X-ray
diffractometer (Bruker, D8 Advance). Raman spectroscopy was performed on a Horiba LabRam
HR Evolution system with a 532 nm laser excitation. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS)
measurements were conducted on a Thermo Fisher ESCALAB XI+ spectrometer using a
monochromatic Al Kα X-ray source. All binding energies were calibrated relative to the
adventitious carbon C 1s peak at 284.8 eV.

Functional Property Measurements
The P-E hysteresis loops and I-E curves were measured on a ferroelectric analyzer (tf analysis
3000E).

Device Fabrication
For two-terminal ferroelectric memristors fabrication, AZ5214 photoresist was spin-coated onto
the sample surface at a rate of 4000 rpm and subsequently baked at 110°C for 2 minutes. The
patterning of the top gate was achieved through UV-lithography (MA6, Karl Suss), followed by
the deposition of 30 nm Au metal via electron beam evaporation. The lift-off process was then
employed to obtain the patterned top electrodes.

For three-terminal ferroelectric transistors fabrication, 5 nm thick hafnium oxide dielectric layer
was grown on the bottom-gate at 150°C using atomic layer deposition (ALD). Following this, the
monolayer MoS film was carefully transferred onto the HfO -WO /Bi WO -Nb:SrTiO substrate.
2 2 3 2 6 3
Next, the MoS channels were defined through UV-lithography and reactive ion etching (RIE),
2
employing the Plasma Lab 80 Plus instrument from Oxford Instruments Company. To fabricate
the device contacts, UV-lithography was utilized to define the contact regions, which were
subsequently metallized with a 30 nm Au through electron beam evaporation.

Device Characterization
Characterization of electrical and optoelectronic properties was performed using a probe station
(Janis ST-500-1-(4CX)) equipped with Agilent semiconductor analyzers (models 4156C and
B1500A).

DFT calculation details
Density functional theory (DFT) calculations were carried out using the generalized gradient
approximation (GGA) for the exchange-correlation potential, the projector augmented wave (PAW)
method, and a plane-wave basis set as implemented in the Vienna ab-initio simulation package
(VASP). The lattice constants of WO were fixed to the experimentally determined values: a =
3
5.34 Å, b = 5.34 Å, c=5.90 Å, respectively. An 8 × 8 × 1 k-mesh was used to sample the first
Brillouin zone. The kinetic energy cut-off for the plane-wave basis was set to 400 eV for the
geometric properties and energy calculations. The atomic positions of the structures were fully
relaxed until the residual force per atom was less than 0.001 eV/Å. A second-order Methfessel–
Paxton smearing method with a sigma value of 0.05 eV was adopted during calculations. The
ferroelectric switching in FE and PE phases, respectively, was investigated utilizing the nudged-
elastic-band (NEB) method.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
The authors present a study based on interfacial engineering where they template metastable WO3 in a BWO matrix to manipulate the direction of polarization within the layered materials crystal structure. This is an interesting known approach to manipulate polar behavior and can be instrumental materials' design for ferroelectric applications. The following suggestions (if implemented) can be beneficial in improving the readability and reproducibility of the manuscript:
(a) References: The authors should consider citing other studies on ferroelectric thin films leveraging a similar nano-structuring strategy as the authors, also known as vertically aligned nanocomposite thin films in some cases. Including such citations can help validate the findings in the manuscript well.
(b) In line 159, the authors mention "The FFT pattern from the BWO region (Figure 2b) exhibit excellent agreement with the known parameters of pristine BWO structure (Figure S3a). The FFT pattern of WO3 closely resemble that of BWO, confirming their structural similarity. Notably, the absence of superlattice spots in WO3 reveals a reduced periodicity along the [001] crystallographic direction compared to BWO. This observation underscores distinct lattice modulation characteristics between the two systems despite their shared structural motifs."
The authors should justify/explain this observation further. It is a bit surprising that despite the structural similarities between BWO and WO3 crystal structures, the lattice modulation characteristics for them are distinct in nature.
(c) The authors should consider comparing and contrasting the macroscopic polarization-electric field behavior (Figure 6a) in WO3/BWO nanocomposite thin films with that for BWO and WO3 films individually in identical device configuration. Such analysis can improve the clarity of the study further.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
In this manuscript, the authors report the synthesis of thin films composed of a mixture of Bi2WO6 (BWO) Aurivillius phase and WO3 (WO) binary oxide. The films exhibit segregated nanocrystalline regions corresponding to the two phases. The authors claim that the WO3 regions are stabilized in a typically metastable phase that exhibits out-of-plane polarization. When combined with the in-plane polarization of the Aurivillius BWO phase, the overall film is proposed to display switchable polarization along both in-plane and out-of-plane directions. Finally, the authors demonstrate potential device integration by embedding the films into ferroelectric FET and memristor-type device structures.
0)The manuscript presents an interesting concept, proposing the use of Aurivillius Bi2WO6 (BWO) as a structural template to achieve out-of-plane polarization in the WO3 phase. While the topic is promising, the current presentation lacks sufficient experimental evidence to convincingly support the claims. The central argument, that BWO serves as a structural template, is not fully substantiated. From the data provided, the BWO and WO3 phases appear to be segregated within the thin film. Consequently, it is unclear how BWO functions as a template for the WO3 phase. In my view, the observed polarization in WO3 is more likely a result of epitaxial strain imposed by the STO substrate rather than a direct templating effect from BWO. A true template effect would require evidence of coherent, lattice-matched growth across the film, rather than phase segregation.
Additionally, the authors attribute the polarization in WO3 to stabilization of the Pca21 phase. However, the phase analysis is very limited, relying primarily on STEM images along a single zone axis. No comprehensive structural characterization (e.g., multi-axis STEM, XRD, or reciprocal space mapping) is presented to rigorously confirm the Pca21 phase or quantify the polar distortion.
Overall, due to the lack of in-depth structural analysis, limited high-quality supporting data, and insufficient experimental details provided, the manuscript does not convincingly support its key claims, required for publication in Nature Communications. I therefore cannot recommend publication in Nature Communications in its current form.
Here are my point-by-point technical comments:
1)I could not find a “Methods” section. Was it submitted elsewhere? Because most of the experimental details of the variety of measurements they perform are missing. Providing these details is critical for assessing the validity and reproducibility of the results.
2)The manuscript does not provide sufficient technical context for its claims. First, the concept of using Aurivillius layered frameworks to create composite materials with properties absent in the pure Aurivillius phases is not new; however, the manuscript fails to acknowledge prior literature. For example, this paper (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-60176-8) reports the synthesis of composite films consisting of Aurivillius Bi5FeTi3O15 and BiFeO3.
Second, the authors provide almost no discussion of strain engineering in WO3 thin films. Numerous studies and recent preprints demonstrate that polar phases in WO3 can be stabilized through epitaxial strain or strain gradients imposed by the substrate https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2505.11021 , DOI: 10.1021/acs.jpclett.3c01546, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-020-18644-w). A detailed analysis of the epitaxial strain from the STO substrate and its potential role in stabilizing the polar phase is necessary to place the work in the proper context and to support the manuscript’s central claims.
3)In lines 60-62, the authors state, “By templating metastable WO3 nanoparticles within a BWO matrix, we simultaneously achieve perpendicular polarization and inherited thermal robustness.”. This description is misleading. The term “nanoparticles” implies isolated, discrete 0D entities, which is not the case here; the WO3 regions are part of a continuous thin film and appear to be phase-segregated rather than discrete particles Furthermore, the use of the term “templating” suggests control over the size, shape, and spatial arrangement of these regions, which is not demonstrated in the manuscript. What is observed is simply a film containing two segregated crystalline phases. No evidence is provided that the BWO phase actively controls or templates the structure of the WO3 phase. As such, the claims regarding nanoparticle templating and the associated functional advantages are not supported by the data.
4)In Figure 1c, the orientation of the AFM cantilever relative to the thin film should be clearly indicated. The polarization directions of the in-plane domains, as well as the in-plane crystallographic axes of the film, should also be labelled. The authors mention four in-plane polarization variants, yet it is unclear why there is no corresponding contrast in the VPFM channel. Some of these variants would be expected to produce a measurable deflection of the cantilever, thus a contrast in VPFM. A comprehensive analysis of in-plane polarization using a series of vector-PFM measurements is necessary to fully characterize the domain structure.
In Figure 1d, critical experimental details are missing. The sign of the applied voltage, the component to which the voltage was applied (tip vs. sample), the cantilever movement path, and the slow scanning axis should all be reported to support claims of switching induced by a trailing field. Based on the images, in-plane switching is not convincingly demonstrated. For example, in the innermost square, the brightest contrast increases, yet in the middle square, the expected increase in the darkest contrast is not observed. Clearly marking the switched regions using dashed lines in the pristine images (Figures 1c-e) would facilitate comparison before and after DC voltage application and improve clarity.
5)In lines 116–117, the authors state that an initial BWO layer was first grown. However, this layer is not clearly visible in the STEM images presented in Figure 2. The manuscript should provide clear evidence of the presence, thickness, and continuity of the BWO layer, as well as any interfaces with the WO3 phase, to support the reported growth sequence.
6)In lines 171–178, the authors discuss a “structural templating effect.” From the STEM images, it appears that the BWO and WO3 phases do not mix and form completely segregated regions within the thin film. Given this lack of intermixing, the system cannot reasonably be described as a “composite” material. Moreover, the STEM images suggest that the WO3 phase grows directly on the STO substrate rather than on or within the BWO regions. Accordingly, the statement in lines 176–178—“This observation provides direct evidence that the WO3 phase grows via a structural templating effect inherited from the BWO matrix”—is misleading. The BWO layer does not appear to act as a template; rather, the epitaxial relationship with the STO substrate likely governs the growth. To support any claim of templating, the authors should provide the FFT of the STO substrate and compare it with the WO3 and BWO regions, to demonstrate that the observed structural alignment is not merely inherited from the STO lattice, which also has a square FFT pattern similar to BWO.
7)Figure 2: The authors should comment on the observation of contrast differences in the designated regions of the film. I.e., the brighter contrast in the WO3 part or the darker contrast regions in BWO. Providing a detailed explanation of the origin of this contrast, whether due to atomic number differences, thickness variations, strain, or imaging conditions, would help clarify the structural interpretation and support the identification of the two phases.
8)In lines 182–185, the authors claim that WO3 retains lattice coherence with the BWO phase. From the presented STEM images, however, it appears that there is a relatively large region at the vertical interface where a transitional crystal structure forms, rather than clear lattice coherency. The authors should provide stronger evidence—such as high-resolution imaging across multiple zones, strain mapping, or FFT analysis—to support any claim of a coherent relationship between the two phases.
9)In lines 186–192, the authors report the stabilization of a new metastable phase in WO3. However, insufficient structural information is provided beyond a qualitative comparison with the ferroelectric HfO2 phase using STEM images. Essential crystallographic parameters, such as the lattice constants (a, b, c), angles (α, β, γ), and unit cell volume, should be reported. To fully characterize this phase, X-ray diffraction analysis is necessary, including both θ–2θ scans and reciprocal space mapping to obtain crystallographic information along all three principal axes. Furthermore, the role of substrate-induced strain should be carefully analysed. The authors should discuss whether the observed metastable phase could instead be stabilized by epitaxial strain from STO, independent of the BWO layer. Such analysis is critical to substantiate claims regarding phase stabilization and the proposed templating effect.
10)In Figure 5, the in-plane domains observed in the LPFM images seem to disappear in the BWO/WO3 film, in contrast to the pure BWO film. However, the STEM images indicate that some regions of the film consist of pure BWO. The authors should clarify what happens to the in-plane polarization in these BWO regions within the composite film. A discussion of how the presence of WO3 affects the in-plane ferroelectric domains of BWO, and whether any depolarization or screening effects occur, is necessary to interpret the LPFM results.
11)In Figure 6, the presented P-V loop appears leaky. To support the claim of ferroelectric switching, the authors should also report the transient switching current alongside the P-V loop. Additionally, essential details of the ferroelectric capacitor structure are missing, including the material and dimensions of the top electrode, the diameter of the top electrode, the type of voltage pulse applied, and the pulse period. Providing these details is necessary to assess the reliability and reproducibility of the reported ferroelectric behaviour.
12)The authors attribute ferroelectricity in WO3 to oxygen displacements, but no direct experimental evidence is provided to support this claim. The current STEM images primarily resolve the cation sublattice and are insufficient to confirm oxygen off-centering. To substantiate the proposed mechanism, a more advanced STEM technique, such as integrated Differential Phase Contrast (iDPC-STEM), is necessary to directly visualize oxygen positions and quantify their displacements.

The cross-sectional STEM images presented in Figure 2 were acquired using a High-Angle
Annular Dark-Field (HAADF) detector. In this imaging mode, the signal intensity (image
contrast) is approximately proportional to the square of the atomic number (Z-contrast).
Therefore, brighter regions correspond to areas with a higher average atomic number.
As the reviewer correctly inferred, the observed contrast originates primarily from
differences in chemical composition, not from thickness variations, as the sample was prepared
to be uniformly thin using focused ion beam (FIB) milling.
The brighter regions are identified as the BWO Aurivillius phase. This is due to the
presence of heavy Bismuth (Bi, Z=83) atoms. Despite containing W (Z=74) atoms, the high
atomic number of Bi dominates the scattering, leading to a strong HAADF signal and bright
contrast.
The darker regions are identified as the WO phase. This phase consists predominantly of
number in these regions, causing weaker electron scattering and thereby producing the darker
contrast observed in the HAADF-STEM images.

observed atomic arrangement aligns remarkably well with our computational model of the

You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

The discovery of novel ferroelectric compounds and the modulation of polarization in
established ferroelectric materials have persistently represented crucial and highly dynamic
areas of research within the field of ferroelectric materials science. Here we demonstrate a
structural templating strategy to reconfigure Aurivillius-phase oxides into metastable
ferroelectric phases with tailored polarization. By stabilizing a metastable WO phase within
3
a Bi WO framework, we achieve robust out-of-plane polarization (10 µC/cm2) in textured
2 6
WO /Bi WO films, contrasting the purely in-plane polarization of pristine Bi WO . First-
3 2 6 2 6
principles calculations and atomic-resolution scanning transmission electron microscopy
unveil a WO phase with oxygen displacement-driven ferroelectricity. Prototype ferroelectric
3
field-effect transistors and memristors fabricated from these films exhibit robust switching
ratios (>106) and thermal stability up to 350°C. This work not only expands the family of
binary ferroelectric oxides but also establishes a generalizable paradigm for overcoming
polarization-directionality constraints in layered ferroelectrics.

---

## Introduction

Ferroelectric materials with switchable polarization are the cornerstone of emerging non-
volatile memory and neuromorphic computing technologies. While perovskite oxides (e.g.,
Pb
0.8
Zr
0.2
TiO
3
, BaTiO
3
, BiFeO
3
) are promising for their large intrinsic polarization1-3, their
incompatibility with silicon processing and depolarization field with reduced dimension hinder
integration. Two-dimensional (2D) ferroelectric materials (e.g., CuInP S 4, In Se 5,6, SnS7, SnTe8,
2 6 2 3
and sliding 2D ferroelectric materials such as WTe
2
9, hBN10, GaSe11) offer considerable
advantages for flexible device applications and the novel assembly of heterostructures, but suffer
from inadequate polarization and poor thermal stability12. Recent advances in HfO -based systems
2
have revived interest in CMOS-compatible ferroelectrics13-16, yet the wake-up effect associated
with their metastable phases persist as critical bottlenecks17-19.

Aurivillius-phase oxides present a unique opportunity to bridge these gaps. Aurivillius-phase
oxides, characterized by its layered perovskite structure with alternating bismuth oxide layers and
perovskite-like structural layers, are distinguished by their fatigue-resistant ferroelectric
switching20,21, high Curie temperature22, and remarkable oxide ion conductivity23. However, most
Aurivillius ferroelectric compounds exhibit in-plane polarization24. Bi WO (BWO), the simplest
2 6
member of this family that consists of alternating [Bi O ]2+ and [WO ]2- layers aligned along the
2 2 4
c-axis, restricts spontaneous polarization to the in-plane (ab) directions25,26. This configuration
fundamentally conflicts with the vertical polarization orientation required by mainstream device
architectures, such as ferroelectric field-effect transistors (FeFETs) and ferroelectric tunnel
junctions (FTJs).

The functional properties of ferroelectric thin films can be engineered through diverse
strategies in heterostructure design. Notable approaches include the use of vertically aligned
nanocomposites to create emergent multiferroicity27-29, the application of interphase strain to
robustly enhance ferroelectric polarization30,31, and more recently, the exploitation of the unique
electrostatic environment within Aurivillius frameworks to stabilize complex ferrielectric orders32.

In this work, we resolve this conflict through interfacial engineering: By templating metastable
WO domains within a BWO matrix, we simultaneously achieve perpendicular polarization and
3
inherited thermal robustness. First-principles calculations and atomic-resolution scanning
transmission electron microscopy (STEM) confirmed the presence of a WO
3
structure with
ferroelectric properties. This metastable WO phase, similar to HfO -based ferroelectrics, belongs
3 2
to the family of binary oxide ferroelectrics. Prototype ferroelectric field-effect transistors and
memristors fabricated from these films exhibit robust switching ratios (>106) and thermal stability
up to 350°C. Our work expands the landscape of simple-oxide ferroelectrics, showing a structural
templating strategy that can reconfigure Aurivillius oxides with controllable polarization
properties.

Pure Bi WO Thin Film
2 6
We start with pure BWO films as the control experiment. In literature reports, high quality

orthorhombic phase structure with lattice constants a = 5.437 Å, b = 5.458 Å, and c = 16.430 Å34.

In our experiment, pure BWO films are grown on 0.7 wt % Nb-doped SrTiO (Nb:STO) (100)

orientation, rotated 45 as compared with Fig. 2. Here the out-of-plane direction is aligned along
[001] and the in-plane direction along [100], respectively. In Fig. 3a, the BWO structure distinctly
shows a layered configuration, featuring alternating Bi-O layers and W-O layers along the c-axis.
The inserted theoretical crystal structure corresponds well with the atomic structure observed in
the STEM images. In contrast, the WO region lacks layering but displaying a square lattice
3
geometry (Fig. 3b). Figs. 3c and 3d show the FFT analysis corresponding to Figs. 3a and 3b, where
Fig. 3c exhibits precise congruence with the reference BWO crystallographic parameters
(Supplementary Fig. 3c). The FFT patterns of the WO phase in Fig. 3d closely resemble those of
3
BWO, apart from the absence of 32 superlattice spots caused by the periodic modulation. This
observation provides direct evidence that the WO phase grows via a structural templating effect
3
inherited from the BWO matrix. To validate the general applicability of the structural templating
mechanism, we synthesized ultrathin films by employing the identical epitaxial growth mode with
a reduced deposition dosage. The 8 nm-thick textured nanocomposite WO /BWO thin film
3
exhibits structural and compositional invariance across its engineered interfaces, as evidenced by
cross-sectional STEM analysis (Supplementary Fig. 4). Importantly, the WO phase forms a semi-
3
coherent epitaxial relationship with the BWO template, demonstrating the robustness of this
templating strategy in governing phase evolution across dimensional scales, further validating the
epitaxial growth and crystallographic alignment of the nanocomposite film.

Notably, this WO structure does not match to any existing WO phase in literature41-43,
3 3
signifying the stabilization of a metastable polymorph. While previous studies have demonstrated
that epitaxial strain from perovskite substrates can homogeneously distorts the bulk WO
3
structure44,45，the formation mechanism here is fundamentally different. This distinction can be
understood by analogy ferroelectric HfO
2
—which adopts a non-ferroelectric monoclinic P2
1
/c
phase at ambient conditions, but exhibits ferroelectricity in its metastable orthorhombic Pca2
1
phase18,46. Crucially, BWO shares this Pca2 ferroelectric space group. This structural templating
1
mechanism is further supported by X-ray diffraction (XRD) and reciprocal space mapping (RSM)
analyses. Conventional θ–2θ scans (Supplementary Fig. 5) reveal no significant peak shifts
between pure BWO and WO /BWO nanocomposite films, which is consistent with the presence
3
of nanosized WO domains whose diffraction is masked by the dominant BWO matrix. In contrast,
3
a pure WO film grown directly on Nb:STO (001) under identical conditions exhibits distinctly
3
different XRD features, corresponding to a conventional monoclinic phase47,48, which confirms
that the metastable polar phase observed in the nanocomposite is not stabilized by the substrate
alone. RSM measurements provide further insight into the strain state of the heterostructure.
Around the STO (001) reflection (Supplementary Figs. 6a,b), the WO /BWO film shows a
3
systematic shift toward lower q , indicating out-of-plane expansion. Consistently, the RSM around
z
the STO (103) reflection (Supplementary Figs. 6c,d) reveals a shift toward higher q accompanied
x
by lower q , confirming in-plane compression coupled with out-of-plane elongation. These RSM
z
results are in excellent agreement with cross-sectional STEM observations (Supplementary Fig.
7), collectively demonstrating that the BWO framework acts as an atomic-scale template, guiding
the WO into a semi-coherent, non-bulk-like configuration stabilized by the host lattice.
3

The BWO structural template provides a shared epitaxial orientation and a local chemical
environment, which directs the WO phase to nucleate and grow into nanodomains with specific
3
crystallographic characteristics, rather than forming randomly oriented or thermodynamically
stable phases. The primary role of the STO substrate is thus to enable the epitaxial growth of a
high-quality BWO template, which in turn architecturally guides the formation of this polar WO
3
phase.

The origin of ferroelectricity
The atomically-resolved TEM images suggest a straightforward structural model as shown in
Fig. 4a. In this model, each W atom is coordinated by five oxygen atoms, forming a pyramid shape,
distorted pentahedral as the structural unit. There are two different types of oxygen atoms in this
structure model. First, four O atoms are located roughly in the same plane with the W atoms (the
bottom plane of the pyramids), where each O atom connects two pyramid units, as marked by the
dotted rectangle and circle in Fig. 4a. Second, there is another O atom sitting at the top site of the
pyramid, which bonds solely to the W atom below it (marked by red arrow in Fig. 4a). In total this
configuration gives a WO stoichiometry, agreeing with our experiments. These WO pyramids
3 5
form a lattice precisely align with experimental TEM images from different views. First-principles
density functional theory (DFT) calculations verify the structural stability of this model.

Remarkably, we find that such an atomic configuration is naturally ferroelectric (FE). In Fig.
4a, all the pyramid units are pointing upward. Structural analysis reveals a Cm space group
configuration that breaks out-of-plane symmetry compared to the centrosymmetric WO
6
octahedral arrangement, generating a substantial out-of-plane spontaneous polarization of ~80
μC/cm2 (Fig. 4c). This polarization magnitude approaches that of prototypical perovskite
ferroelectrics, including BiFeO (100 μC/cm2)49,50 and significantly exceeds that of BaTiO (26
3 3
μC/cm2)51,52. More interestingly, the structural model naturally suggests the coexistence of a
paraelectric phase (PE), where half of the pyramid units are flipped (Fig. 4b). The reversed
polarization in neighboring layers results in zero net polarization in this phase. If all the pyramids
are flipped, it will result in the switching between the ferroelectric states (from FE' to FE'').

First-principles Nudged Elastic Band (NEB) simulations employing a 2×2×1 supercell unveil
a multi-stage polarization reversal pathway. Fig. 4e illustrates the energy profile for dipole
switching, where Fig. 4d shows the two states before and after flipping from FE'' to FE'. The
computed activation energy barrier for individual oxygen migration approximates 330 meV,
indicating practical feasibility for electric-field-induced polarization switching. This energy
landscape suggests that the ferroelectric transition proceeds through a concerted mechanism
involving sequential atomic displacements rather than simultaneous collective motion.
Additionally, the ferroelectricity is achieved here through oxygen sublattice engineering in a
simpler binary oxide system, different from conventional perovskites. The combination of giant
spontaneous polarization and moderate switching barriers positions this WO phase as a promising
3
candidate for non-volatile memory applications.

To further corroborate the consistency between the computational and experimental results,
we performed diffraction pattern simulations along the [1̅10] and [010] crystallographic directions
for the theoretically optimized structure. As shown in Supplementary Figs. 3b and 3d, the
simulated FFT patterns exhibit excellent agreement with the experimental data presented in Figs.
2d and 3d, validating the structural fidelity of the computational models and their alignment with
the observed lattice configurations.

Perpendicular Ferroelectricity of the textured nanocomposite WO /Bi WO film.
3 2 6
Indeed, the most remarkable finding with our textured nanocomposite WO /BWO films is their
3
robust ferroelectricity with perpendicular polarization. We employed PFM for a comprehensive
analysis of their ferroelectric response. The conductive Nb:STO substrate allows us to ground the
substrate and ensure the application of a vertical electric field to the thin films for out-of-plane
polarization measurements. A pre-designed badminton pattern was utilized during the PFM
scanning process (Fig. 5f), where white regions correspond to the application of a positive voltage
(+8 V) by the PFM tip, and black regions represent a negative voltage (-8 V). During point-by-
point scanning of the thin film surface with the AFM tip, voltages were applied according to this
pattern. Figs. 5a,b show the resulting out-of-plane PFM amplitude and phase after the electric field
was applied. Point-by-point scanning across the film surface resulted in distinct ferroelectric
domains, as observed both in the out-of-plane PFM amplitude and phase images. The amplitude
image shows minimized polarization at domain walls, which are formed between regions of
opposite polarization. Meanwhile, the phase image reveals a clear 180° phase shift between
adjacent domains, with black areas indicating upward polarization and yellow areas representing
downward polarization. Analysis of the PFM amplitude and phase data (Fig. 5c) along the red
dashed lines in Figs. 5a,b clearly indicates minimized polarization amplitude at the domain walls,
with a phase difference of 180° between the adjacent domains, thereby confirming the excellent
out-of-plane ferroelectric properties of the fabricated thin films. Supplementary Fig. 8 also
demonstrates comparable out-of-plane polarization switching characteristics in the 8 nm thick
nanocomposite film, further illustrating the low-dimensional nature of the ferroelectric thin films
constructed in this work.

In addition to out-of-plane measurements, in-plane PFM amplitude and phase images were
also recorded (Figs. 5d,e). The images demonstrate variations in in-plane ferroelectric polarization,
primarily induced by the trailing electric effect of the PFM tip during the scanning process. This
observation indicates that the thin films exhibit both out-of-plane and in-plane ferroelectric
polarization. Notably, higher-resolution imaging (Supplementary Fig. 9) confirms that the
characteristic in-plane ferroelectric domain structure of the BWO matrix remains clearly
resolvable at finer scan scales, demonstrating its preservation within the nanocomposite
architecture. Furthermore, to evaluate the stability and reliability of the ferroelectric switching, we
conducted polarization switching curve tests at a single PFM tip point (Fig. 5g). Ten consecutive
measurements revealed highly stable and repeatable ferroelectric hysteresis and butterfly loops,
with a consistent phase difference of 180° and a switching threshold voltage of approximately 4 V.
These results highlight the robust ferroelectric switching performance of the thin films.

To eliminate potential artifacts and verify the authenticity of the observed ferroelectric
properties, we performed alternating current (AC) voltage-dependent polarization switching
measurements (Fig. 5h). When the applied AC voltage exceeds 3 V, close to the threshold voltage
for ferroelectric switching, the polarization hysteresis loop collapsed, this behavior confirms the
genuine nature of the out-of-plane ferroelectric polarization in the textured nanocomposite
WO /BWO film53. Additionally, temperature-dependent polarization curve tests were conducted
3
to assess the films' thermal stability (Fig. 5i). Measurements were performed from room
temperature up to the maximum operating temperature of 250°C, where the polarization switching
curves exhibited robust stability despite minor jitter caused by temperature-induced contact
instability between the tip and the sample. These results collectively demonstrate the exceptional
durability and performance of our textured nanocomposite WO /BWO thin films under varying
3
thermal conditions.

Performance of ferroelectric FET and memristor devices made from WO /Bi WO films
3 2 6
Our textured nanocomposite WO /BWO thin films exhibit also macroscopic ferroelectricity,
3
as measured by a ferroelectric analyzer. Fig. 6a displays the measured ferroelectric hysteresis loop,
from which the key ferroelectric parameters were quantitatively extracted. Specifically, at an
applied electric field of 4 MV/cm, the film exhibits a remnant polarization (P) of approximately
r
10 μC/cm2, accompanied by a coercive field (E ) of 2.5 MV/cm. Since the out-of-plane
c
ferroelectric polarization in these films primarily originates from the WO domains, the measured
3
value is lower than that of the pure ferroelectric WO calculated in Fig. 4c (80 μC/cm2). The
3
macroscopic ferroelectric hysteresis loop serves as direct evidence for the presence of out-of-plane
polarization in the nanocomposite films, suggesting that these ferroelectric thin films hold
significant potential for applications in electronic devices.

To further showcase the potential device performance based on our films, we deposited a 5 nm
thick HfO insulating layer on the as-grown films using atomic layer deposition (to minimize
2
leakage effects during testing, the leakage currents primarily originate from oxygen vacancy
defects introduced during the growth of the oxide films, as well as conducting pathways formed
along interface within the textured film.) and subsequently transferred a monolayer MoS
2
via a dry
transfer method. Fig. 6b illustrates the schematic diagram of the complete device structure, for
which a FeFET characterization was conducted. Fig. 6c presents the double-sweep transfer
characteristics of the device, obtained by scanning the back-gate voltage (V
GS
) from −1.5 V to +5
V and then back to −1.5 V at a fixed drain voltage (V ) of 1 V. The FeFET exhibits a high on/off
DS
current ratio of 3×106, demonstrating its excellent performance. Then, we deposited gold
electrodes on the film surface to investigate the memristive effect induced by out-of-plane
ferroelectric polarization. Fig. 6d shows the schematic of the ferroelectric memristor device, while
Fig. 6e presents the current-voltage (I-V) characteristics under voltage sweeps ranging from -5 V
to +5 V. The device transits from the initial high-resistance state (HRS) to a low-resistance state
(LRS) after a 0 to +5 V sweep, maintains LRS during the subsequent +5 V to -5 V scan, and returns
to HRS from -5 V to 0 V. We further conducted high-temperature tests demonstrating robust
memristive behavior across a wide temperature range from 100°C to 350°C (Fig. 6f), highlighting
the potential of our ferroelectric thin films for high-temperature memory applications. This
comprehensive analysis highlights the promising capabilities of the fabricated textured
nanocomposite WO /BWO films for advanced electronic applications, supported by both
3
macroscopic ferroelectric measurements and device-level performance evaluations.

In summary, we demonstrate a structural engineering strategy to achieve out-of-plane
ferroelectricity in a metastable WO phase derived from the Aurivillius oxide BWO framework.
3
Through a combination experiments and first-principles calculations, we have confirmed the
existence of this previously unreported ferroelectric WO phase. The resulting textured
3
nanocomposite WO /BWO thin films exhibit both out-of-plane and in-plane ferroelectric
3
polarization, showcasing stable and repeatable switching behavior. Prototype FeFETs and
ferroelectric memristors fabricated from the films exhibit remarkable switching ratios (>106)
coupled with robust thermal stability up to 350°C. This work not only expands the family of binary
ferroelectric oxides but also provides a generalizable approach for polarization enhancement in
Aurivillius oxides and other layered ferroelectrics.

---

## Methods

Thin film growth
Bi WO , WO /Bi WO and WO thin films were epitaxially grown on (001)-oriented Nb:SrTiO
2 6 3 2 6 3 3
(0.7% wt. doped) substrates by pulsed laser deposition using a 248 nm KrF excimer laser. The
deposition was carried out at a substrate temperature of 750℃ under an oxygen environment of
400 mtorr. The laser energy density and repetition rate were maintained at approximately 1.4 J cm-
2 and 2 Hz, respectively. After deposition, the samples were cooled down to room temperature in
7.5 torr of O with a cooling rate of 5 °C/min.
2

Piezoresponse force microscopy (PFM)
PFM measurements were performed using an Oxford Instruments Cypher (E)S atomic force
microscope, equipped with conductive Pt/Ir-coated silicon probes. The local electromechanical
response was characterized in both out-of-plane and in-plane directions using AC excitation
amplitudes of 800 mV at frequencies of 350 kHz and 650 kHz, respectively. Litho-PFM mode was
utilized to locally pole the material and write domain patterns by applying a DC bias through the
scanning tip, enabling the assessment of polarization switching. Spectroscopic PFM (SS-PFM)
measurements were performed in dual AC resonance tracking (DART) mode. In this mode, an AC
excitation signal was superimposed on a series of DC triangular and sawtooth waveform voltages
to track the bias-dependent electromechanical response.

Scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM)
Cross-sectional specimens for STEM were prepared by focused ion beam (FIB) lift-out and
subsequently thinned using a Gatan 691 PIPS for final ion milling. High-angle annular dark-field
(HAADF) STEM imaging was performed on an aberration-corrected (scanning) transmission
electron microscope (JEOL, Grand ARM 300) operated at an accelerating voltage of 300 kV.

Materials Characterization
X-ray θ–2θ scan and reciprocal space mappings were performed using a high-resolution X-ray
diffractometer (Bruker, D8 Advance). Raman spectroscopy was performed on a Horiba LabRam
HR Evolution system with a 532 nm laser excitation. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS)
measurements were conducted on a Thermo Fisher ESCALAB XI+ spectrometer using a
monochromatic Al Kα X-ray source. All binding energies were calibrated relative to the
adventitious carbon C 1s peak at 284.8 eV.

Functional Property Measurements
The P-E hysteresis loops and I-E curves were measured on a ferroelectric analyzer (tf analysis
3000E).

Device Fabrication
For two-terminal ferroelectric memristors fabrication, AZ5214 photoresist was spin-coated onto
the sample surface at a rate of 4000 rpm and subsequently baked at 110°C for 2 minutes. The
patterning of the top gate was achieved through UV-lithography (MA6, Karl Suss), followed by
the deposition of 30 nm Au metal via electron beam evaporation. The lift-off process was then
employed to obtain the patterned top electrodes.

For three-terminal ferroelectric transistors fabrication, 5 nm thick hafnium oxide dielectric layer
was grown on the bottom-gate at 150°C using atomic layer deposition (ALD). Following this, the
monolayer MoS film was carefully transferred onto the HfO -WO /Bi WO -Nb:SrTiO substrate.
2 2 3 2 6 3
Next, the MoS channels were defined through UV-lithography and reactive ion etching (RIE),
2
employing the Plasma Lab 80 Plus instrument from Oxford Instruments Company. To fabricate
the device contacts, UV-lithography was utilized to define the contact regions, which were
subsequently metallized with a 30 nm Au through electron beam evaporation.

Device Characterization
Characterization of electrical and optoelectronic properties was performed using a probe station
(Janis ST-500-1-(4CX)) equipped with Agilent semiconductor analyzers (models 4156C and
B1500A).

DFT calculation details
Density functional theory (DFT) calculations were carried out using the generalized gradient
approximation (GGA) for the exchange-correlation potential, the projector augmented wave (PAW)
method, and a plane-wave basis set as implemented in the Vienna ab-initio simulation package
(VASP). The lattice constants of WO were fixed to the experimentally determined values: a =
3
5.34 Å, b = 5.34 Å, c=5.90 Å, respectively. An 8 × 8 × 1 k-mesh was used to sample the first
Brillouin zone. The kinetic energy cut-off for the plane-wave basis was set to 400 eV for the
geometric properties and energy calculations. The atomic positions of the structures were fully
relaxed until the residual force per atom was less than 0.001 eV/Å. A second-order Methfessel–
Paxton smearing method with a sigma value of 0.05 eV was adopted during calculations. The
ferroelectric switching in FE and PE phases, respectively, was investigated utilizing the nudged-
elastic-band (NEB) method.
